title: AP Biology — Q1 Class Notes
subtitle: Handwritten notes practice · Themes through respiration
subject: AP Biology

questions.prompt: How do the notes define an organism’s genome? ((notes, PDF1 p.01))

options.text: The entire library of genetic instructions that an organism inherits.
Only the genes that are transcribed into mRNA in a given cell type.
The set of proteins produced by translation in one tissue.
A single chromosome that carries all of an organism’s traits.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.01). The genome is defined as the entire library of genetic instructions that an organism inherits.

questions.prompt: In the biological hierarchy from largest to smallest, which sequence is correct? ((notes, PDF1 p.01))

options.text: Biosphere → Ecosystem → Communities → Populations → Organisms → Organs → Tissues → Cells → Organelles → Molecules.
Molecules → Cells → Tissues → Organs → Organisms → Populations → Communities → Ecosystem → Biosphere → Organelles.
Biosphere → Populations → Communities → Ecosystem → Organisms → Organs → Tissues → Cells → Organelles → Molecules.
Ecosystem → Biosphere → Communities → Populations → Organisms → Tissues → Organs → Cells → Molecules → Organelles.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.01). The notes list the hierarchy largest → smallest as Biosphere → Ecosystem → Communities → Populations → Organisms → Organs → Tissues → Cells → Organelles → Molecules.

questions.prompt: Which set matches the seven properties of life listed in the notes? ((notes, PDF1 p.01))

options.text: Order; energy processing; regulation; growth and development; evolutionary adaptation; response to the environment; reproduction.
Order; energy processing; regulation; growth and development; photosynthesis; response to the environment; reproduction.
Order; energy processing; regulation; multicellularity; evolutionary adaptation; response to the environment; reproduction.
Order; energy processing; regulation; growth and development; evolutionary adaptation; response to the environment; locomotion.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.01). Life is recognized by what living things do; the seven listed properties are order, energy processing, regulation, growth and development, evolutionary adaptation, response to the environment, and reproduction.

questions.prompt: Along the DNA → protein path in the notes, which step correctly pairs process and product? ((notes, PDF1 p.02))

options.text: DNA → mRNA is transcription; mRNA → amino acid chain is translation; amino acid chain → protein is folding.
DNA → mRNA is translation; mRNA → amino acid chain is transcription; amino acid chain → protein is folding.
DNA → protein is transcription; mRNA → amino acid chain is folding; amino acid chain → mRNA is translation.
DNA → mRNA is protein folding; mRNA → amino acid chain is transcription; amino acid chain → protein is translation.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.02). The notes map DNA → mRNA (transcription), mRNA → chain of amino acids (translation), and chain of amino acids → protein (protein folding).

questions.prompt: According to the notes, what are the three domains of life? ((notes, PDF1 p.04))

options.text: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya.
Bacteria, Protista, and Animalia.
Archaea, Fungi, and Plantae.
Bacteria, Eukarya, and Viruses.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.04). The three domains of life are Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya.

questions.prompt: How do negative and positive feedback differ in regulating biological systems? ((notes, PDF1 p.04))

options.text: Negative feedback returns the system toward homeostasis (the norm); positive feedback moves the system away from homeostasis.
Positive feedback returns the system toward homeostasis; negative feedback moves the system away from the norm.
Both negative and positive feedback always return the system to homeostasis.
Negative feedback only occurs in evolution; positive feedback only occurs in DNA replication.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.04). Feedback mechanisms regulate biological systems: negative feedback brings the system back to homeostasis, while positive feedback moves it away from the norm.

questions.prompt: Beyond being an educated guess, what must a scientific hypothesis be? ((notes, PDF1 p.05))

options.text: It must be specific and testable.
It must already be proven true before any experiment begins.
It must rely only on inductive observation and never on if…then statements.
It must describe a discovery-based record of nature without predicting outcomes.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.05). A hypothesis is more than an educated guess: it is specific and must be testable, and hypotheses gain credibility as they survive attempts to falsify them.

questions.prompt: In the mimicry bar-graph results, how did attack patterns on artificial snakes change when coral snakes were present versus absent? ((notes, PDF1 p.06))

options.text: When coral snakes were absent, artificial kingsnakes took most attacks (~83%); when coral snakes were present, brown artificial snakes took most attacks (~84%).
When coral snakes were absent, brown artificial snakes took most attacks (~83%); when coral snakes were present, artificial kingsnakes took most attacks (~84%).
Artificial kingsnakes and brown artificial snakes each received about 50% of attacks whether coral snakes were present or absent.
When coral snakes were present, artificial kingsnakes received nearly all attacks (~83%), matching the absent condition.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.06). With coral snakes absent, artificial kingsnakes ~83% of attacks vs brown ~17%; with coral snakes present, artificial kingsnakes ~16% vs brown ~84%.

questions.prompt: Which set of elements does the notes summarize as essential for life using the CHONPS mnemonic? ((notes, PDF1 p.09))

options.text: Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur.
Carbon, helium, oxygen, neon, phosphorus, and silicon.
Calcium, hydrogen, oxygen, nickel, potassium, and sodium.
Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, potassium, and sodium only.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.09). Essential elements for life are summarized as CHONPS: C, H, O, N, P, and S.

questions.prompt: How do atomic number and mass number differ? ((notes, PDF1 p.10))

options.text: Atomic number equals the number of protons; mass number equals the sum of protons and neutrons.
Atomic number equals the number of neutrons; mass number equals the number of electrons only.
Atomic number equals protons plus neutrons; mass number equals the number of protons only.
Atomic number equals electrons in the outer shell; mass number equals the number of isotopes.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.10). Atomic number is the number of protons; mass number is the sum of protons and neutrons.

questions.prompt: What makes isotopes of the same element different from one another? ((notes, PDF1 p.10))

options.text: They have a different number of neutrons.
They have a different number of protons, so they are different elements.
They always have a different number of electrons in every shell.
They differ only in electronegativity, not in particle counts.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.10). Isotopes are atoms that have a different number of neutrons; radioactive isotopes are used for dating the age of matter.

questions.prompt: In covalent bonding, what is electronegativity? ((notes, PDF1 p.11))

options.text: The attraction of a particular atom for the electrons of a covalent bond.
The complete transfer of valence electrons from one atom to another to form ions.
The number of protons that defines an element’s atomic number.
The sharing of a full octet of electrons between two identical atoms only.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.11). Covalent bonds share a pair of valence electrons; electronegativity is the attraction of a particular atom for the electrons of a covalent bond.

questions.prompt: How do water molecules interact through hydrogen bonding, per the notes? ((notes, PDF1 p.13))

options.text: Water is polar and forms hydrogen bonds with other molecules; each water molecule can hydrogen-bond to four more water molecules.
Water is nonpolar and forms covalent bonds to four other water molecules at once.
Water forms ionic bonds between H+ and OH− instead of hydrogen bonds.
Each water molecule hydrogen-bonds to only one other water molecule, never more.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.13). Water is a polar molecule that forms hydrogen bonds (not covalent bonds) with other molecules; every one water molecule can hydrogen-bond to four more.

questions.prompt: Which emergent properties of water are listed as contributing to Earth’s suitability for life? ((notes, PDF1 p.13))

options.text: Cohesion, adhesion, surface tension, and specific heat.
Hydrophobicity, radioactivity, surface tension, and specific heat.
Cohesion, adhesion, ionic bonding, and electronegativity.
Cohesion, adhesion, surface tension, and atomic number.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.13). Emergent properties of water include cohesion, adhesion, surface tension, and specific heat (water has a very high specific heat).

questions.prompt: How do acids, bases, and buffers relate to H+/OH− and pH in the notes? ((notes, PDF1 p.15))

options.text: An acid increases H+ in a solution; a base increases OH−; a buffer can absorb H+ or OH− and resist a pH change.
An acid increases OH− in a solution; a base increases H+; a buffer always shifts pH by tenfold.
An acid and a base both decrease H+ equally; buffers only work at pH 0.
Acids and bases do not change ion concentrations; buffers permanently fix pH at 14.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.15). An acid increases H+; a base increases OH−; a buffer absorbs H+ or OH− without changing the solution’s pH (example: the ocean).

questions.prompt: What ecological impact of acid rain do the notes emphasize? ((notes, PDF1 p.16))

options.text: Acid rain affects ecosystems such as lakes and forests.
Acid rain only raises ocean salinity and does not affect lakes or forests.
Acid rain strengthens cohesion of water in plant xylem and never harms ecosystems.
Acid rain converts all lakes into buffers that permanently hold pH at 7.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.16). Acid rain affects ecosystems such as lakes and forests (industrial gases create acidic conditions; the quiz stem focuses on the ecosystem effect).

questions.prompt: In dehydration synthesis, how are polymers assembled? ((notes, PDF1 p.19))

options.text: Monomers join into polymers and water is lost in the process.
Polymers break apart into monomers and water is consumed.
Monomers join into polymers only when water is added as a reactant.
Polymers form by ionic attraction without covalent bonds or water change.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.19). Dehydration synthesis creates polymers with loss of water; hydrolysis is the water-requiring breakdown.

questions.prompt: How do lipids differ from the other major macromolecule classes? ((notes, PDF1 p.20))

options.text: They are the only class of macromolecules not considered polymers.
They are the only class built exclusively from amino-acid monomers.
They are the only hydrophilic macromolecules in cells.
They are the only macromolecules that never appear in membranes.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.20). Lipids (fats, triglycerides, phospholipids, steroids) are hydrophobic and are the only macromolecule class not treated as polymers; they are major membrane components.

questions.prompt: What is a glycosidic bond? ((notes, PDF1 p.20))

options.text: A covalent bond formed between two or more monosaccharides.
An ionic bond that holds fatty acids to glycerol.
A hydrogen bond between complementary nitrogen bases in DNA.
A peptide bond linking amino acids into a polypeptide.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.20). Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides join by dehydration; the covalent link is a glycosidic bond.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly describes structural polysaccharides? ((notes, PDF1 p.20))

options.text: Cellulose in plants; chitin in arthropods and fungi.
Glycogen in plants; cellulose in animals.
Chitin as the main storage polysaccharide in animal muscle.
Cellulose as the storage polysaccharide that animals deposit in liver.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.20). Structural polysaccharides: cellulose (plants) and chitin (arthropods and fungi). Storage roles belong with glycogen (animals), not cellulose.

questions.prompt: Which polysaccharide is correctly paired with its storage role in animals? ((notes, PDF1 p.20))

options.text: Glycogen — storage polysaccharide in animals.
Cellulose — storage polysaccharide in animals.
Chitin — storage polysaccharide in animals.
Cholesterol — storage polysaccharide in animals.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.20). Notes list glycogen as the animal storage polysaccharide; cellulose and chitin are structural, not storage.

questions.prompt: Which statement about fats and fatty acids matches the notes? ((notes, PDF1 p.20))

options.text: A triglyceride is 1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids; saturated fatty acids lack C–C double bonds and are solid at room temperature.
A triglyceride is 1 glycerol + 2 fatty acids; saturated fatty acids have many C–C double bonds and are liquid at room temperature.
A triglyceride is 3 glycerols + 1 fatty acid; unsaturated fatty acids never contain double bonds.
Fats are hydrophilic polymers of glucose; fatty acids lack carboxyl groups.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.20). Fat/triglyceride = 1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids. Saturated: no C–C double bonds, solid at room temp. Unsaturated: C–C double bonds, liquid at room temp.

questions.prompt: Which description correctly matches a level of protein structure? ((notes, PDF1 p.22))

options.text: Secondary structure: hydrogen bonding that forms α helices and β sheets.
Tertiary structure: only the interaction of helix and pleated sheet with no side-chain role.
Primary structure: folding of multiple polypeptide subunits into one protein.
Quaternary structure: the unique linear sequence of amino acids alone.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.22). Primary = unique amino-acid sequence; secondary = H-bonding into α helix and β sheets; quaternary = 2+ polypeptide chains. The notes’ tertiary wording (helix/pleated only) is oversimplified and is not used as correct.

questions.prompt: Which nitrogen-base statement correctly contrasts DNA and RNA? ((notes, PDF1 p.23))

options.text: Thymine occurs only in DNA; uracil occurs only in RNA.
Uracil occurs only in DNA; thymine occurs only in RNA.
Adenine is found only in DNA; guanine is found only in RNA.
Cytosine is found only in RNA; guanine is found only in DNA.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.23). Nitrogen bases include adenine and guanine (purines), cytosine, thymine (DNA only), and uracil (RNA only).

questions.prompt: What is energy coupling? ((notes, PDF1 p.08))

options.text: Using the products of an exergonic reaction to help run an endergonic reaction.
Combining two endergonic reactions so both absorb free energy with no driver.
Defining an exergonic reaction as one that produces a net gain of free energy.
Separating anabolic and catabolic pathways so they never share intermediates.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF1 p.08). Energy coupling uses the products of an exergonic reaction to help run an endergonic reaction; ATP hydrolysis of the terminal phosphate releases energy for that coupling.

questions.prompt: What is metabolism, as defined in the notes? ((notes, PDF1 p.07))

options.text: The collection of all chemical reactions that occur within an organism.
Only the reactions that release heat from an ecosystem to space.
The single reaction that converts ATP into glucose for long-term storage.
The physical movement of organisms without any chemical change.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.07). Metabolism is the collection of all chemical reactions (rxns) within an organism.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly matches a law of thermodynamics from the notes? ((notes, PDF1 p.07))

options.text: Second law: every energy transfer increases the entropy (disorder) of the universe.
First law: every energy transfer decreases the entropy of the universe.
Second law: energy can neither be created nor destroyed but can change forms.
First law: endergonic reactions always increase entropy without energy input.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.07). 1st law: energy neither created nor destroyed (changes form). 2nd law: every energy transfer increases entropy of the universe.

questions.prompt: How do enzymes speed up metabolic reactions? ((notes, PDF3 p.08))

options.text: By lowering energy barriers.
By permanently raising the ΔG of every reaction they catalyze.
By destroying substrates so reactions cannot reverse.
By adding heat until the cell reaches boiling temperature.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF3 p.08). Enzymes speed up metabolic reactions by lowering energy barriers; regulation of enzyme activity helps control metabolism.

questions.prompt: When the terminal phosphate bond of ATP is broken, what happens? ((notes, PDF1 p.08))

options.text: Energy is released and ATP becomes ADP.
Energy is absorbed and ADP becomes ATP with no phosphorylation step.
ATP gains a fourth phosphate and stores more free energy.
ATP converts directly into a polysaccharide without releasing energy.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.08). Breaking ATP’s terminal (last) phosphate bond releases energy; ATP becomes ADP. ADP can later be phosphorylated to reform ATP.

questions.prompt: How do temperature and pH affect enzymes, per the notes? ((notes, PDF1 p.24))

options.text: Each enzyme has an optimal temperature; large pH shifts can denature the enzyme.
Enzymes work equally well at every temperature and pH with no optimum.
Only salt concentration matters; temperature and pH never affect enzyme shape.
Denaturation requires removing the enzyme’s allosteric site permanently from the gene.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.24). Environmental factors temper enzyme activity: each enzyme has an optimal operating temperature; increases or decreases in pH can denature enzymes.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme–action pairing matches the notes’ enzyme table? ((notes, PDF1 p.24))

options.text: Kinase — transfers a phosphate group; lipase — breaks down lipids.
Lipase — transfers a phosphate group; kinase — breaks down lipids.
Kinase — adds CO2 to form a −COOH group on any molecule.
Lipase — removes CO2 from any molecule as its only action.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.24). Lipase: substrate lipids, breaks down lipids. Kinase: substrate any molecule, transfers a phosphate group. (Carboxylase wording in the notes is flagged and not used as correct.)

questions.prompt: Which pairing of enzyme-regulation ideas matches the notes? ((notes, PDF1 p.24))

options.text: Allosteric site: where a regulator binds; feedback inhibition: pathway end product inhibits an enzyme.
Allosteric site: identical to the active site; feedback inhibition: substrate permanently destroys the enzyme.
Feedback inhibition: first substrate of a pathway always activates every enzyme; allosteric sites do not bind regulators.
Allosteric regulation only occurs after the enzyme is fully denatured by extreme pH.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava handwritten notes (notes, PDF1 p.24). Allosteric site: portion of the enzyme where a regulator binds. Feedback inhibition: end product of a biological pathway inhibits the enzyme.

questions.prompt: How do the notes calculate total magnification on a light microscope? ((notes, PDF2 p.01))

options.text: Total magnification = ocular magnification × objective magnification.
Total magnification = ocular magnification + objective magnification.
Total magnification = objective magnification ÷ ocular magnification.
Total magnification equals only the highest objective lens power.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.01). Ocular lenses are 10× and objectives are 4×, 10×, 40×, or 100×; total magnification is ocular × objective. Cytology is defined on the same page as the structure and function of cells.

questions.prompt: Which contrast between light and electron microscopes matches the notes? ((notes, PDF2 p.01))

options.text: A light microscope can view prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells but not viruses; an electron microscope uses a beam of electrons for greater magnification and resolution.
A light microscope can view viruses but not eukaryotic cells; an electron microscope uses ordinary white light only.
Both light and electron microscopes can resolve viruses equally well; they differ only in cost.
An electron microscope cannot improve resolution; a light microscope routinely resolves viruses.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.01). Light microscopes view prok/euk cells but not viruses; electron microscopes use an electron beam for greater magnification and resolution.

questions.prompt: What do the notes say about the nucleoid region of a prokaryotic cell? ((notes, PDF2 p.02))

options.text: It is devoid of a true nucleus; DNA floats in the cytoplasm.
It is a double-membrane nucleus that houses linear chromosomes.
TEM views it as the cell surface; SEM views it as internal organelles.
It is the site of protein synthesis on membrane-bound ribosomes.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.02). Prokaryotes lack a nucleus; the nucleoid is where DNA floats in the cytoplasm. (Same page: TEM views organelles; SEM views cell surfaces — used here only as a distractor contrast.)

questions.prompt: Which structures do the notes list as present in plant cells but not in animal cells? ((notes, PDF2 p.04))

options.text: Cell wall, chloroplast, central vacuole, and plasmodesmata.
Centrioles, lysosomes, flagella, and intermediate filaments.
Nucleoid region with DNA floating freely and a sugar capsule only.
Rough ER, Golgi apparatus, and mitochondria.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.04). Plant-only structures listed are cell wall, chloroplast, central vacuole, and plasmodesmata. Prokaryote nucleoid (no true nucleus; DNA in cytoplasm) is on PDF2 p.02.

questions.prompt: How do smooth ER and rough ER differ in the notes? ((notes, PDF2 p.14))

options.text: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and synthesizes lipids and carbohydrates (and detoxifies drugs); rough ER has ribosomes and synthesizes proteins and new membranes.
Smooth ER has ribosomes and makes proteins; rough ER lacks ribosomes and only stores DNA.
Both smooth and rough ER lack ribosomes and function only in phagocytosis.
Rough ER detoxifies drugs; smooth ER is the only site of translation.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.14). Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and handles lipids/carbohydrates/detoxification; rough ER has ribosomes and synthesizes proteins and new membranes.

questions.prompt: Which statement about lysosomes matches the notes? ((notes, PDF2 p.15))

options.text: They contain hydrolytic enzymes that break down macromolecules and work best at a low pH.
They synthesize lipids and detoxify drugs and work best at a high pH.
They stack thylakoids into grana and produce ATP in the light reaction.
They transfer hydrogen to make H₂O₂ and then use catalase to make water.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.15). Lysosomes hold hydrolytic enzymes for breaking down macromolecules; those enzymes work best at a low pH. (Thylakoid/grana and peroxisome/catalase appear as distractors from nearby organelle notes.)

questions.prompt: Which statement about mitochondria matches the notes? ((notes, PDF2 p.15))

options.text: The inner membrane is folded into cristae, and mitochondrial DNA is inherited from mother to child.
Mitochondria lack their own DNA and inherit all genes only from the father.
Mitochondria are stacks of thylakoids called grana in the chloroplast.
Mitochondria are made of alpha and beta tubulin and drive pinocytosis.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.15). Inner membrane folded into cristae; mitochondrial inheritance is always mother → child.

questions.prompt: Which microtubule-related statement matches the notes? ((notes, PDF2 p.16))

options.text: Microtubules are made of alpha and beta tubulin and are involved in mitosis; cilia and flagella have a 9+2 configuration.
Centrioles have a 9+3 configuration that correctly describes their microtubule arrangement.
Microtubules are made of actin protein and are used only for pinocytosis.
Cilia and flagella both have a 9+0 configuration and lack tubulin.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.16). Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.16–17). Microtubules = α/β tubulin and are involved in mitosis; cilia and flagella have a 9+2 configuration. Centriole “9+3” is audit-flagged and used only as a distractor. Prokaryote nucleoid (DNA floating in cytoplasm, no true nucleus) is on PDF2 p.02.

questions.prompt: How do integral and peripheral membrane proteins differ in the notes? ((notes, PDF2 p.04))

options.text: Integral proteins are transmembrane proteins with hydrophobic and hydrophilic portions; peripheral proteins bind to integral proteins on the outside of the membrane.
Peripheral proteins span the bilayer; integral proteins only float freely in the cytosol.
Integral proteins bind only to cholesterol; peripheral proteins carry out osmosis alone.
Both types are identical transmembrane channels that invert across the bilayer.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.04). Integral = transmembrane with hydrophobic and hydrophilic portions; peripheral bind to integral proteins on the outside of the membrane.

questions.prompt: What is the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane according to the notes? ((notes, PDF2 p.04))

options.text: The membrane is a mosaic of proteins that float around in the phospholipids; membranes are not static and move laterally but never invert.
The membrane is a rigid sheet of cellulose with proteins locked in fixed positions.
The membrane is only cholesterol molecules stacked in a static bilayer.
The membrane is a sugar capsule outside the cell wall with no proteins.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.04). Fluid mosaic: proteins float among phospholipids; membranes move laterally but do not invert.

questions.prompt: What role does cholesterol play in membranes per the notes? ((notes, PDF2 p.04))

options.text: Cholesterol is found in membranes and helps the membrane be less fluid.
Cholesterol is found in membranes and makes the membrane more fluid.
Cholesterol forms the sugar capsule outside the prokaryotic cell wall.
Cholesterol is the only molecule that can cross the membrane by osmosis.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.04). Cholesterol is present in membranes and assists the membrane in being less fluid.

questions.prompt: Which molecules do the notes say can cross the membrane with relative ease? ((notes, PDF2 p.05))

options.text: Small hydrophobic / nonpolar molecules such as O₂ and CO₂.
Large charged molecules such as proteins and ions.
Only water, and only when ATP is hydrolyzed.
Only sugars, and only through the nuclear pores.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.05). Small hydrophobic/nonpolar molecules such as O₂ and CO₂ cross with relative ease; large and charged molecules face selective permeability.

questions.prompt: How do the notes describe the direction of diffusion of solute relative to tonicity? ((notes, PDF2 p.08))

options.text: Solute flows from a hypertonic (concentrated) solution to a hypotonic (dilute) solution — the inverse direction of osmosis.
Solute flows from a hypotonic solution to a hypertonic solution — the same direction as osmosis.
Solute only moves when ATP is used; diffusion never follows a concentration difference.
Solute always moves into the cell in a hypertonic environment and out in a hypotonic one.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.08). Diffusion: solute from hypertonic (concentrated) to hypotonic (dilute); notes mark osmosis and diffusion as inversely related in direction.

questions.prompt: In which direction does osmosis move water according to the notes’ tonicity framing? ((notes, PDF2 p.08))

options.text: Water flows from a hypotonic solution to a hypertonic solution (iso: even flow; hypo: water in; hyper: water out).
Water flows from a hypertonic solution to a hypotonic solution only.
Water never moves; only solute always moves from hypo to hyper.
Hypotonic means higher solute concentration, so water always leaves a hypotonic side.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.08). Isotonic: water flows evenly; hypo: water flowing in; hyper: water flowing out; osmosis is water from hypotonic → hypertonic. Distractor D echoes the swapped p.05 solute defs and is not treated as correct.

questions.prompt: How do facilitated diffusion and active transport differ in the notes? ((notes, PDF2 p.12))

options.text: Facilitated diffusion moves molecules (usually polar) with a transport protein and is passive (no energy); active transport moves against the concentration gradient and requires ATP.
Facilitated diffusion requires ATP; active transport is always passive and needs no protein.
Both are identical forms of endocytosis that engulf solids and fluids.
Facilitated diffusion only moves O₂ and CO₂; active transport only moves water by osmosis.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.12). Facilitated diffusion is passive protein-aided movement; active transport moves against the gradient using ATP.

questions.prompt: Which matching of bulk-transport terms matches the notes? ((notes, PDF2 p.12))

options.text: Exocytosis secretes materials out by vesicle fusion; endocytosis takes materials in by vesicles; phagocytosis engulfs molecules; pinocytosis is “cell drinking” of fluids or small molecules.
Exocytosis takes materials in; endocytosis secretes materials out; phagocytosis is cell drinking; pinocytosis engulfs large solids only.
Phagocytosis and pinocytosis are both forms of active transport that require no vesicles.
Endocytosis and exocytosis are both types of facilitated diffusion across channel proteins.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 notes, (notes, PDF2 p.12). Exocytosis = vesicle fusion secreting out; endocytosis = taking in via vesicles; phagocytosis = engulfs molecules; pinocytosis = cell drinking of fluids/small molecules.

questions.prompt: When light acts as a particle, packets of energy emitted are called what? ((notes, PDF2 p.18))

options.text: Photons (packets of light energy).
Pigments only — colored molecules with no energy packets.
Grana (stacks of thylakoids), not energy packets.
Stomata (leaf pores), not energy packets.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 handwritten notes, (notes, PDF2 p.18). When light acts as a particle it emits packets of energy known as photons.

questions.prompt: According to the notes, chlorophyll absorbs which wavelengths and reflects which color that we see? ((notes, PDF2 p.19))

options.text: Absorbs red or blue light; reflects green light.
Absorbs green light; reflects red and blue light.
Absorbs only yellow light; reflects white light.
Absorbs all visible wavelengths equally; reflects none.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 handwritten notes, (notes, PDF2 p.19). Chlorophyll absorbs red or blue light but reflects green light (which we see).

questions.prompt: How do the notes contrast short-term energy carriers with long-term storage in photosynthesis? ((notes, PDF2 p.19))

options.text: ATP and NADPH act like short-term "taxi cab" carriers; glucose is long-term storage.
Glucose is the only short-term carrier; ATP is long-term storage in the stroma.
Only NADPH stores energy long-term; ATP and glucose are discarded as waste.
Chlorophyll itself is the long-term carbohydrate store; ATP is never formed.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 handwritten notes, (notes, PDF2 p.19). Energy-storing compounds: ATP and NADPH as "taxi cab" carriers; glucose for long-term storage.

questions.prompt: What is the main product of the light-independent reaction as framed in the notes? ((notes, PDF2 p.20))

options.text: Glucose (longer-term energy storage)
Oxygen gas released before any carbon fixation
Only water split at the reaction center
Bundle-sheath cells that open stomata at night

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 handwritten notes, (notes, PDF2 p.20). The light-independent reaction uses stored energy from ATP/NADPH to produce glucose (longer-term energy storage).

questions.prompt: How is O2 produced during the light reactions according to the notes? ((notes, PDF2 p.21))

options.text: Chlorophyll replaces lost electrons by stripping water of H+, releasing O2.
CO2 is split in the stroma, releasing O2 before carbon fixation.
Glucose is oxidized in the thylakoid, releasing O2 as a byproduct.
NADPH donates oxygen atoms that exit through stomata as O2.

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 handwritten notes, (notes, PDF2 p.21). To replace electrons that went into NADPH, chlorophyll strips water of H+, releasing O2 into the atmosphere.

questions.prompt: Where do the notes say the dark reaction (glucose production using ATP and NADPH) takes place? ((notes, PDF2 p.21))

options.text: In the stroma
In the thylakoid space only
In the mitochondrial matrix
In the cytoplasm outside the chloroplast

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 handwritten notes, (notes, PDF2 p.21). The dark reaction uses ATP and NADPH to make glucose and takes place in the stroma.

questions.prompt: How do CAM plants manage stomata and CO2 collection in the notes? ((notes, PDF2 p.23))

options.text: Stomata closed during the day; open at night to collect CO2 and store it in vacuoles
Stomata open only at midday so PEP can bind O2 instead of CO2
Stomata stay open continuously; CO2 never enters vacuoles
Stomata close at night; all CO2 fixation occurs only in mitochondria

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 handwritten notes, (notes, PDF2 p.23). CAM plants keep stomata closed during the day and open during the night to collect CO2 and store it in vacuoles.

questions.prompt: Which adaptation do C4 plants use, per the notes, to support the Calvin cycle? ((notes, PDF2 p.23))

options.text: Bundle-sheath cells and PEP to increase CO2 for the Calvin cycle
Keeping stomata closed all night and never fixing CO2
Storing CO2 only as lactic acid in the cytoplasm
Running the entire Calvin cycle in the mitochondrial matrix

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 handwritten notes, (notes, PDF2 p.23). C4 plants have bundle-sheath cells and use phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to increase CO2 for the Calvin cycle.

questions.prompt: How do alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation differ in the notes? ((notes, PDF3 p.01))

options.text: Alcoholic: ethyl alcohol byproduct (e.g. yeast); lactic acid: lactic acid byproduct (cheese/yogurt; can occur in human cells)
Alcoholic: lactic acid in muscle; lactic acid: ethyl alcohol in yeast only
Both produce O2 as the main byproduct and require aerobic ETS
Neither produces ATP; both only regenerate chlorophyll

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 handwritten notes, (notes, PDF3 p.01). Alcoholic fermentation produces ATP with ethyl alcohol (yeast; wine/baking); lactic acid fermentation produces ATP with lactic acid (cheese, yogurt; can be used by human cells).

questions.prompt: Where do the electron transport system and chemiosmosis occur, and which protein is used in chemiosmosis? ((notes, PDF3 p.01))

options.text: Inner mitochondrial membrane foldings; ATP synthase
Cytoplasm only; Rubisco
Stroma of the chloroplast; PEP carboxylase
Nuclear envelope; collagen

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 handwritten notes, (notes, PDF3 p.01). ETS and chemiosmosis (oxidative phosphorylation) take place in the inner mitochondrial membrane folding; ATP synthase is the protein used in chemiosmosis.

questions.prompt: Which description correctly matches the three junction types in the notes? ((notes, PDF3 p.04))

options.text: Tight: join plasma membranes in a sheet; anchoring: link cytoskeletons; communication: allow direct cell-to-cell signaling connections
Tight: link cytoskeletons only; anchoring: open channels for CO2; communication: seal plasma membranes shut permanently

Tight: ethyl alcohol export; anchoring: lactic acid export; communication: ATP synthase only

questions.explanation: Source: Ava Q1 handwritten notes, (notes, PDF3 p.04). Tight junctions connect plasma membranes of adjacent cells in a sheet; anchoring junctions connect cytoskeletons; communication junctions allow communication with adjacent cells through direct connections.
